items.prompt: What is the "virtual DOM"?
choices: A lightweight, in-memory representation of what the UI should currently look like, compared against the previous version to compute minimal real DOM changes
A backup copy of the real DOM stored on the server
A separate DOM tree used only for print stylesheets
The browser's internal representation of CSS specificity rules
items.explanation: The virtual DOM is an in-memory comparison target used to compute the smallest set of real DOM changes needed — not a server backup, print-specific tree, or CSS mechanism.

items.prompt: Why do frameworks compare a virtual DOM instead of applying every change directly to the real DOM?
choices: To compute the minimal set of real DOM changes needed, since real DOM operations are more expensive than in-memory comparisons
Because browsers don't allow direct DOM manipulation from JavaScript at all
Because the virtual DOM is required for CSS to apply correctly
Because real DOM changes can only happen once per page load
items.explanation: The virtual DOM exists specifically to minimize costly real DOM operations by computing the smallest necessary change set first.

items.prompt: What is "diffing" (reconciliation) in this unit's context?
choices: The process of comparing an old and new virtual DOM tree to determine exactly what changed
The process of minifying JavaScript before deployment
The process of resolving merge conflicts in version control
The process of compressing images for faster page loads
items.explanation: Diffing/reconciliation is specifically about comparing two UI states to find the actual differences — unrelated to minification, version control, or image compression.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, deleting one contact out of 5,000 caused the diff to detect changes across thousands of rows. What does this suggest about how the diff was comparing items?
choices: It was likely comparing items by position rather than by a stable identity
It was comparing items alphabetically regardless of position
It was re-fetching the entire list from the server on every change
It was comparing items by their exact pixel coordinates on screen
items.explanation: Position-based comparison is exactly what makes a single deletion look like thousands of changes, since every item after the deleted one shifts into a 'different' position.

items.prompt: What is a "key" in the context of list rendering?
choices: A stable identifier attached to each item in a rendered list, used to match an item in the new list back to the same item in the old list regardless of position
A password required to modify a list's contents
The primary sort field used to order a list alphabetically
A CSS class applied to highlight the currently selected list item
items.explanation: A key is specifically for identity-matching during diffing — not authentication, sorting, or styling.

items.prompt: Would giving every row in the Scenario's list a stable key based on each contact's id fix the described bug?
choices: Yes — with keys, the diff can match each item to itself regardless of position, so deleting one contact produces only one real change
No — keys have no effect on how diffing compares list items
No — keys only affect the visual styling of list items, not diffing behavior
Yes, but only if the list has fewer than 100 items
items.explanation: Stable, identity-based keys are exactly what let the diff recognize unmoved items as unchanged, regardless of how their position shifted.

items.prompt: What is "reflow"?
choices: The browser recalculating the position and size of elements after a layout-affecting change
The browser re-downloading a page's CSS file
The browser clearing its cache
The browser re-parsing the page's HTML from scratch
items.explanation: Reflow is specifically layout recalculation — not a network re-fetch, cache operation, or HTML re-parse.

items.prompt: What is "repaint"?
choices: The browser redrawing the pixels for elements whose appearance changed
The browser recompiling JavaScript for better performance
The browser resizing the entire browser window
The browser switching between light and dark mode
items.explanation: Repaint is specifically about redrawing pixels after a visual change — not JS compilation, window resizing, or theme switching.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, was the actual logical change (deleting one contact) large or small?
choices: Small — exactly one contact was removed, and every other contact was unchanged
Large — deleting one contact required recalculating every other contact's data
It's impossible to tell how large the logical change was
The change was large because 5,000 contacts had to be re-fetched from the server
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that only one contact was removed and every other contact was unchanged — the visible stutter came from how that small change was diffed, not from the change itself being large.

items.prompt: Why did the Scenario's bug feel invisible with only 5 contacts but visible with 5,000?
choices: The same position-based diffing pattern produces far more operations as the list grows, even though the underlying logical change (one deletion) stays the same size
The bug only exists in production environments, never in development
5 contacts and 5,000 contacts use fundamentally different diffing algorithms
The bug didn't actually exist with 5 contacts — it was introduced later by a code change
items.explanation: The pattern's cost scales with how many items sit after the deleted one — small at 5 items, dramatic at 5,000, even though the same algorithm runs in both cases.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, why does comparing items by position make a shift look like a change?
choices: Once one item is removed, every subsequent item occupies a different position than before, so a position-only comparison sees a mismatch at each of those positions
Position-based comparison always ignores content entirely, so it can never detect real changes
Position-based comparison only works correctly for lists shorter than 10 items
Position-based comparison requires re-fetching data from the server for each position
items.explanation: L2's diagram shows exactly this: a shift in position, with no actual content change, still reads as 'the content at this position changed' under pure positional comparison.

items.prompt: Per L2, what question does a stable key let the diffing algorithm ask instead of "did the item at this position change"?
choices: "Where did the item with this specific id end up?"
"What color is the item at this position?"
"How many total items are in the list?"
"What was the very first item in the original list?"
items.explanation: L2 frames the key-based question as tracking a specific item's identity across renders, not asking about color, count, or the first item specifically.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what triggers reflow specifically?
choices: Adding/removing elements, changing dimensions, or changing text content length
Changing only the text color of an element
Changing only the opacity of an element
Loading a new font file
items.explanation: Reflow is triggered by layout-affecting changes (structure, size, content length) — a pure color or opacity change is repaint/composite territory, not reflow.

items.prompt: Per L2, why is reflow generally considered worse for performance than repaint or composite?
choices: Reflow can cascade — recalculating one element's layout can force recalculating its neighbors and ancestors too, affecting a wider scope
Reflow is a legacy browser feature that modern browsers no longer optimize at all
Reflow only happens once per page load, so it's rare but always catastrophic
Reflow and repaint always cost exactly the same amount of time
items.explanation: L2 explains reflow's cascading nature — layout changes can ripple outward, making its scope harder to contain than a purely visual repaint or composite step.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, does using the array index as a key actually fix the position-based diffing problem?
choices: No — the index shifts along with position exactly like no key at all, so it doesn't restore identity-based matching
Yes — using the index as a key is a fully correct and recommended fix
Yes, but only for lists with fewer than 1,000 items
No, because array indices can't be used as keys in any framework
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns that index-as-key looks like a fix but isn't — the index is just as position-dependent as having no key, so identity still isn't tracked correctly.

items.prompt: Per L2, is a small computed diff guaranteed to produce a fast visible update?
choices: Usually, but not guaranteed — the diff result still has to go through the browser's rendering pipeline, and not every kind of change costs the same
Yes — a small diff always means an instantly fast visible update with zero further cost
No — diff size has absolutely no relationship to visible update speed
Yes, but only if the diff was computed using a virtual DOM specifically
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that a small diff is usually fast but not a strict guarantee — the resulting real DOM operations still have to be applied and go through reflow/repaint.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, why might a render-performance bug go unnoticed during development?
choices: Testing only with small, dev-sized lists can make an inefficiency invisible even though the underlying algorithmic behavior hasn't changed
Development environments automatically disable virtual DOM diffing
Render-performance bugs can only occur in production builds, never in development builds
Small lists use an entirely different, bug-free diffing algorithm
items.explanation: The same diffing pattern runs at any list size — the bug's cost, not its existence, is what changes with scale, which is exactly why small dev-sized tests can miss it.

items.prompt: What does L2 recommend to actually catch a diffing-related performance issue before it reaches production?
choices: Testing render performance with data volumes closer to production scale, not just small development-sized lists
Avoiding lists entirely in favor of single large text blocks
Disabling the virtual DOM and manipulating the real DOM directly for every change
Only testing on the fastest available development machine
items.explanation: L2's failure mode is specifically about testing at unrepresentative scale — the fix is testing at data volumes that actually resemble production, not avoiding lists or bypassing the virtual DOM.

items.prompt: Fix diffUnkeyed so it correctly compares two lists position by position, producing an "update" op wherever the ids at a given position differ, plus create/remove ops for any length mismatch.

tests.description: deleting item id 3 from a 5-item list produces 3 ops (position-based shifting)
tests.expr: expect(diffUnkeyed([{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }, { id: 4 }, { id: 5 }], [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 4 }, { id: 5 }]).length).toBe(3)

tests.description: two identical lists produce zero ops
deleting item id 5 from a 10-item list produces 6 ops
tests.expr: expect(diffUnkeyed(Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })), Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })).filter((x) => x.id !== 5)).length).toBe(6)

items.explanation: Comparing purely by position means that once one item is deleted, every subsequent item now sits at a position that held a different id before — each of those positions registers as an 'update,' producing far more ops than the single logical deletion that actually happened.
items.reference:
📍 Position-based — compares slot N's old content to slot N's new content
❌ Result — a shift reads as a change at every shifted position

Why: position alone can't distinguish 'this item changed' from 'this item just moved.'

items.prompt: Fix diffUnkeyed so it correctly compares two lists position by position, producing an "update" op wherever the ids at a given position differ, plus create/remove ops for any length mismatch.

tests.description: deleting item id 4 from an 8-item list produces 5 ops
tests.expr: expect(diffUnkeyed(Array.from({ length: 8 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })), Array.from({ length: 8 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })).filter((x) => x.id !== 4)).length).toBe(5)

tests.description: two identical lists produce zero ops
deleting item id 12 from a 20-item list produces 9 ops
tests.expr: expect(diffUnkeyed(Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })), Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })).filter((x) => x.id !== 12)).length).toBe(9)

items.explanation: Same shape regardless of list size: once one item is deleted, every subsequent position now holds a different id than before, and each of those positions registers as an 'update' under pure positional comparison.
items.reference:
📍 Position-based — compares slot N's old content to slot N's new content
❌ Result — a shift reads as a change at every shifted position

Why: position alone can't distinguish 'this item changed' from 'this item just moved.'

items.prompt: Fix diffKeyed so it correctly compares two lists by id, producing only a "remove" op for ids missing from the new list and a "create" op for ids new to the new list — regardless of position shifts.

tests.description: deleting item id 3 from a 5-item list produces exactly 1 op
tests.expr: expect(diffKeyed([{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }, { id: 4 }, { id: 5 }], [{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 4 }, { id: 5 }]).length).toBe(1)

tests.description: deleting item id 5 from a 10-item list still produces exactly 1 op
tests.expr: expect(diffKeyed(Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })), Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })).filter((x) => x.id !== 5)).length).toBe(1)

tests.description: two identical lists (same ids, same order) produce zero ops

items.explanation: Matching by id means every item that exists in both lists is recognized as the same item no matter where it now sits — only ids that genuinely disappeared or genuinely appeared produce an op, which is why one real deletion produces exactly one op regardless of list size.
items.reference:
🔑 Identity-based — tracks each item by its stable id, not its slot
✅ Result — a shift produces no op at all; only real additions/removals do

Why: identity survives a position change, which is exactly what a stable key is for.
